strengths: The problem motivating this work is important, and to the best of my knowledge this algorithm seems like a novel contribution
Many parts of the paper that are nicely written, including the motivations outline in section 1, and discussion in section 3.
The math discussed in the work, e.g., 4.1 and 4.2 did not seem to have errors.
The number / types of environments seems adequate to provide rankings between algorithms (in aggregation)
The work is tackling a relevant (offline RL) problem that should be of interest to the a non-trivial section of the ICRL community.
The English is easy to understand and the math is (as far as can tell) sound.

The proposed solution - the combination of control-as-inference and Bayesian inference over dynamics - is non-trivial and novel. In particular, it attempts to leverage uncertainty in (offline model-free) policy and (offline model-based) dynamics in a computationally feasible way. Though I am not familiar with the offline RL community/literature, the question on how to combine model-free and model-based is a long and important one in RL. The way it is proposed here "makes sense": a policy pre-trained should be considered a prior, and fine-tuning this online when new data comes in a Bayesian fashion is (only in hindsight) an obvious one.
The Reflect-then-Plan (RefPlan) framework combines Bayesian modeling of epistemic uncertainty with model-based planning in a unified probabilistic approach.

Clear and principled proposal for offline MBRL: The model distribution is learnt via variational inference, while the policy planning step takes into account this model uncertainty to plan for optimal actions to act under epistemic uncertainty.
Clear writing: It's easy to follow and understand both the technical part, e.g. maths behind, and the main proposal, e.g. Fig. 2 has a clear depiction of the proposal.

The incorporation of uncertainty estimation into the offline model-based planning framework is well done, mathematically. As far as I know, this is the first work to do so under the variational inference framework.
Accounting for changes during deployment in the real environment is important in practice. In this sense, this work is well motivated.
The empirical performance is promising and well verifies the adaptivity of the proposed method.
weaknesses: The paper could be improved with more clarity on a lot of the background; many algorithms / ideas were mentioned then cited, having a fuller description of these works in the paper (main body or appendix) would be beneficial, especially when these are used in the main algorithm or often referenced (e.g., BAMDP, control-as-inference framework, quantifying epistemic uncertainty). Specifically, the paper should elaborate on how these concepts are used within the Ref-Plan framework, how the control-as-inference framework specifically informs the planning process, and how the Bayesian approach to uncertainty quantification is implemented and what specific assumptions are made.

Further explanation connecting the environment settings chosen and resulting epistemic uncertainty (RQ1) would improve the flow; the paper should provide a more detailed explanation of why the chosen initialization strategy leads to high epistemic uncertainty and what specific aspects of the environment or dataset cause this uncertainty.

The distinction between the sources of epistemic uncertainty in RQ1, RQ3, and RQ4 is not sufficiently clear; the paper should explicitly state what specific aspects of the experimental setup in each RQ lead to the claimed type of epistemic uncertainty, clarifying how subsampling the dataset in RQ3 leads to epistemic uncertainty about the environment's dynamics versus the uncertainty caused by OOD initialization in RQ1, and how changes in environment dynamics in RQ4 differ from RQ1 and RQ3.
The last comment in alg2 refers to line 5 in alg1, but there are no line numbers; line 5 specifically is the beginning of a loop.
It is unclear what error bars are used in the experiments.
The meaning of bold vs underline in Table 1 is unclear.
H-step is mentioned without being defined.

Important concepts were not clearly defined (e.g. "epistemic POMDPs", "BA-MDPs"); some concepts that are clearly background (e.g. "control-as-inference") were not introduced, making it excessively hard to infer what was novel and should be credited as well as scrutinized.

A major concern is the lack of experiments for online learning; it is unclear whether planning saves computation or gains information over time, and the experiments only show initial performance, raising the question whether this performance could have been trained/reached offline instead.

The experiments do not include the meta‑learning setting assumed by VariBAD; it is unclear whether the "Bayesian" argument holds, as the encoder might collapse when all trajectories come from the same environment, and the proposed method does not seem to have the Bayesian trait of taking optimal actions with respect to uncertainty.

The paper uses VariBAD's VAE structure to learn environment dynamics but lacks strong evidence that the agent has learned a near Bayes‑optimal policy; it is recommended to add theoretical support or include a navigation task with visualizations of the agent's behavior.

The paper lacks innovation; the approach of offline model‑based planning as probabilistic inference is common (see [1]), and the proposed algorithm is merely a minor modification of VariBAD, lacking novelty. Related work in offline meta‑RL has shown adaptation and generalization across multiple tasks, which is more valuable than the single‑task generalization problem addressed here (see [2][3]).
The paper evaluates the algorithm on only three tasks, which is insufficiently persuasive, and the experimental results show only marginal improvements over LOOP.

It is questionable that RefPlan only fine‑tunes a baseline policy; it is unclear why the learned model can be used to optimize a new policy, and this may be unfair in terms of extra computation needed in comparisons to baselines, especially since the model learned using model‑based methods in the baseline will be discarded or unnecessarily unused in the fine‑tuning stage of RefPlan.
Performance is mixed: RefPlan performs well on some tasks but improvements are not obvious on others (e.g., Hopper), and the gap to existing SOTA (LOOP) is not significant.
Figure 1 is misleading as it could be understood that a GM is input to the encoder; the observed nodes used as data and the graph connection are unclear.

It is unclear how RefPlan compares conceptually to the deterministic and stochastic paths in PlaNet and Dreamer models; the plan is solved using sampling, which may lead to higher variance due to outer sampling with respect to random variable "model m".
Some ablations are needed to understand the effect of the whole sampling step, e.g., the trade‑off between variance and performance and the needed computation.

The sentence "In the offline setting, we aim to enhance the prior policy πp via MB planning at test time by inferring the posterior over" decouples policy and model; it could be revised to compute optimal policies directly from model‑based policy optimization and include a comparison to this baseline.
In Section 5.1 the results are encouraging but it is hard to understand the effect of each component (e.g., visualization of uncertain region) and how the policy is selected in such situations.
APE‑V (Ghosh et al., 2022) seems like a valid baseline for adaptive offline algorithms, however the paper does not compare with it, making the evaluation potentially incomplete and less convincing.
It seems like the hyperparameters need to be carefully tuned for each task, which might limit the usability of the proposed method.
